description: Deeper number-theoretic functions (arithmetic functions, quadratic residues, primitive roots, representations, lattice reduction, algebraic numbers) together with the permutation-group machinery (named groups, orbits, stabilizers, group properties) and combinatorial sequences not covered in the basic discrete-math chunk.

tools.name: CoprimeQ
tools.description: Tests whether integers are pairwise relatively prime (GCD 1). Faster and clearer than GCD[a, b] == 1 and works on any number of arguments and on lists via Listable behaviour.
tools.usage:
CoprimeQ[a, b]
CoprimeQ[n1, n2, n3, ...]

tools.name: PrimePowerQ
tools.description: Tests whether an integer is a power p^k of a single prime; SquareFreeQ tests whether no square factor divides it. Both are standard predicates in number-theoretic sieves and in checks for finite-field orders.
tools.usage:
PrimePowerQ[n]
SquareFreeQ[n]

tools.name: PrimeOmega
tools.description: PrimeOmega[n] counts prime factors with multiplicity (big Omega) and PrimeNu[n] counts distinct prime factors (little omega); both are Listable arithmetic functions used in analytic number theory and in Liouville/Moebius computations.
tools.usage:
PrimeOmega[n]
PrimeNu[n]

tools.name: RandomPrime
tools.description: Generates a random prime in a range (or up to a maximum), optionally several at once. Use it for cryptographic examples, hashing moduli and randomized number-theory tests.
tools.usage:
RandomPrime[{imin, imax}]
RandomPrime[imax]
RandomPrime[{imin, imax}, n]

tools.name: MangoldtLambda
tools.description: The von Mangoldt function: Log[p] if n is a power of the prime p, 0 otherwise. LiouvilleLambda gives (-1)^PrimeOmega[n] and CarmichaelLambda the exponent of the multiplicative group mod n (smallest lambda with a^lambda == 1 for all a coprime to n). These arithmetic functions appear in prime-counting estimates and RSA parameter checks.
tools.usage:
MangoldtLambda[n]
LiouvilleLambda[n]
CarmichaelLambda[n]

tools.name: MultiplicativeOrder
tools.description: Gives the smallest k with k^... i.e. the multiplicative order of a modulo n (least k > 0 with a^k == 1 mod n), or the order relative to a set of residues. Used for period of repeating decimals, cycle lengths of LCGs and discrete-log preprocessing.
tools.usage:
MultiplicativeOrder[a, n]
MultiplicativeOrder[a, n, {r1, r2, ...}]

tools.name: PrimitiveRoot
tools.description: Gives the smallest primitive root modulo n (a generator of the multiplicative group), or the smallest one above a given value; PrimitiveRootList gives all of them. Needed for Diffie-Hellman parameters, number-theoretic transforms and cyclic-group constructions.
tools.usage:
PrimitiveRoot[n]
PrimitiveRoot[n, k]
PrimitiveRootList[n]

parameters.name: n
parameters.description: Modulus (primitive roots exist for 1, 2, 4, p^k, 2 p^k).

parameters.name: k
parameters.description: Return the smallest primitive root >= k.

tools.name: JacobiSymbol
tools.description: The Jacobi symbol (n/m) generalizing the Legendre symbol to odd composite m, with KroneckerSymbol extending to all integers. They decide quadratic residuosity and drive the Solovay-Strassen test and square-root-mod-p algorithms.
tools.usage:
JacobiSymbol[n, m]
KroneckerSymbol[n, m]

parameters.name: m
parameters.description: Odd positive integer (any integer for KroneckerSymbol).

tools.example:
JacobiSymbol[2, 7] (* 1: 2 is a QR mod 7 *)
Select[Range[10], JacobiSymbol[#, 11] == 1 &]
tools.notes: For prime m a value of 1 means n is a quadratic residue; PowerMod[n, 1/2, p] computes the square root.

tools.name: SquaresR
tools.description: SquaresR[d, n] counts the representations of n as a sum of d squares (order and signs distinct); PowersRepresentations[n, k, p] lists the representations of n as a sum of k p-th powers of non-negative integers. Classic tools for Lagrange/Jacobi-type problems and taxicab numbers.
tools.usage:
SquaresR[d, n]
PowersRepresentations[n, k, p]

tools.name: IntegerExponent
tools.description: Gives the highest power of b (default 10) dividing n, i.e. the b-adic valuation; IntegerLength gives the number of digits of n in base b. Use them for trailing-zero counts, p-adic arguments and digit-width formatting.
tools.usage:
IntegerExponent[n]
IntegerExponent[n, b]
IntegerLength[n]
IntegerLength[n, b]

tools.name: DigitCount
tools.description: Counts occurrences of each digit (or of a specific digit) in the base-b representation of an integer; IntegerReverse reverses the digits. Useful for digit-based puzzles, checksums and Benford-type analyses.
tools.usage:
DigitCount[n]
DigitCount[n, b]
DigitCount[n, b, d]
IntegerReverse[n]
IntegerReverse[n, b]

tools.name: BernoulliB
tools.description: Bernoulli numbers B_n and Bernoulli polynomials B_n(x); EulerE gives Euler numbers/polynomials and LucasL the Lucas numbers/polynomials. They appear in Euler-Maclaurin summation, Faulhaber's formula, zeta values and combinatorial identities.
tools.usage:
BernoulliB[n]
BernoulliB[n, x]
EulerE[n]
EulerE[n, x]
LucasL[n]
LucasL[n, x]
tools.example:
BernoulliB[12] (* -691/2730 *)
Sum[k^4, {k, 1, n}] == (BernoulliB[5, n + 1] - BernoulliB[5])/5 // Simplify
LucasL[10] (* 123 *)

tools.name: FrobeniusNumber
tools.description: Gives the largest integer not representable as a non-negative integer combination of the given coprime integers (the coin problem); FrobeniusSolve lists all representations of a target. Applications include change-making, semigroup theory and integer programming examples.
tools.usage:
FrobeniusNumber[{a1, a2, ...}]
FrobeniusSolve[{a1, a2, ...}, b]
FrobeniusSolve[{a1, ...}, b, n]

tools.name: PartitionsQ
tools.description: Counts partitions of n into distinct parts (PartitionsP counts all partitions). Both are fast for huge n via asymptotic and recurrence methods; IntegerPartitions enumerates the partitions themselves.
tools.usage: PartitionsQ[n]
tools.example:
PartitionsQ[10] (* 10 *)
IntegerPartitions[10, All, Range[10], DuplicateFreeQ] // Length

tools.name: DivisorSum
tools.description: DivisorSum[n, f] sums f[d] over the divisors d of n (optionally only those satisfying a condition), a compact form of Total[f /@ Divisors[n]] that is efficient for large n; PerfectNumber[k] gives the k-th perfect number.
tools.usage:
DivisorSum[n, f]
DivisorSum[n, f, cond]
PerfectNumber[k]
PerfectNumberQ[n]
tools.example:
DivisorSum[12, #^2 &] (* DivisorSigma[2, 12] = 210 *)
DivisorSum[30, Identity, PrimeQ] (* 10 *)
PerfectNumber[4] (* 8128 *)

tools.name: FromContinuedFraction
tools.description: Reconstructs a number from its continued-fraction expansion {a0, a1, a2, ...} (periodic parts given as a nested list give quadratic irrationals); ContinuedFractionK represents symbolic continued fractions. Inverse of ContinuedFraction and used in Diophantine approximation and Pell equations.
tools.usage:
FromContinuedFraction[{a0, a1, a2, ...}]
FromContinuedFraction[{a0, {p1, p2, ...}}]
ContinuedFractionK[f, g, {i, imin, imax}]

parameters.name: {a0, a1, ...}
parameters.description: Partial quotients; a trailing list denotes the periodic part.

tools.name: LatticeReduce
tools.description: Computes an LLL-reduced basis of the integer lattice spanned by the rows of a matrix, giving short nearly orthogonal vectors. Applications: integer relation finding, knapsack cryptanalysis, simultaneous Diophantine approximation and finding small solutions of linear congruences.
tools.usage: LatticeReduce[{v1, v2, ...}]

parameters.name: {v1, v2, ...}
parameters.description: Integer (or rational) basis vectors as rows.

tools.example: LatticeReduce[{{1, 0, 0, 10^6 Round[10^6 Pi]}, {0, 1, 0, 10^6 Round[10^6 E]}, {0, 0, 1, 10^6 Round[10^6 (Pi + E)]}}] (* finds relation Pi + E - (Pi+E) *)
tools.notes: HermiteDecomposition and SmithDecomposition give the Hermite and Smith normal forms of integer matrices.

tools.name: HermiteDecomposition
tools.description: Gives {u, r} with r the Hermite normal form of an integer matrix m and u unimodular such that u.m == r; SmithDecomposition gives {u, r, v} with r the Smith normal form (diagonal with divisibility chain). Both are the integer analogues of row reduction, used for solving linear Diophantine systems and computing abelian group invariants.
tools.usage:
HermiteDecomposition[m]
SmithDecomposition[m]

tools.name: AlgebraicNumber
tools.description: Represents an element of an algebraic number field as a polynomial in a generating Root; ToNumberField converts algebraic numbers into a common field, MinimalPolynomial gives the minimal polynomial and RootReduce simplifies expressions in radicals to a canonical Root form. Together they support exact arithmetic beyond rationals.
tools.usage:
AlgebraicNumber[theta, {c0, c1, ...}]
ToNumberField[{a1, a2, ...}]
ToNumberField[a, theta]
MinimalPolynomial[a, x]
RootReduce[expr]
RootApproximant[x]

parameters.name: theta
parameters.description: Generator (a Root object or algebraic number).

tools.example:
MinimalPolynomial[Sqrt[2] + Sqrt[3], x] (* 1 - 10 x^2 + x^4 *)
RootReduce[(1 + Sqrt[5])/2]
ToNumberField[{Sqrt[2], Sqrt[3]}]
RootApproximant[1.618033988749895] (* GoldenRatio candidate *)

tools.name: NumberFieldDiscriminant
tools.description: Gives the discriminant of the algebraic number field generated by an algebraic number; NumberFieldIntegralBasis, NumberFieldClassNumber, NumberFieldFundamentalUnits, NumberFieldRegulator, NumberFieldSignature and NumberFieldRootsOfUnity give the other standard invariants. Use them in algebraic number theory computations.
tools.usage:
NumberFieldDiscriminant[a]
NumberFieldIntegralBasis[a]
NumberFieldClassNumber[a]
NumberFieldFundamentalUnits[a]

parameters.name: a
parameters.description: Algebraic number generating the field, e.g. Sqrt[-5].

tools.name: DirichletCharacter
tools.description: DirichletCharacter[k, j, n] gives the value at n of the j-th Dirichlet character modulo k, and DirichletL[k, j, s] the corresponding Dirichlet L-function; ZetaZero[n] gives the n-th nontrivial zero of the Riemann zeta function. Core objects of analytic number theory.
tools.usage:
DirichletCharacter[k, j, n]
DirichletL[k, j, s]
ZetaZero[n]
ZetaZero[n, t]
tools.example:
Table[DirichletCharacter[5, 2, n], {n, 0, 9}]
DirichletL[4, 2, 1] (* Pi/4 *)
N[ZetaZero[1]] (* 1/2 + 14.1347 I *)

tools.name: Primes
tools.description: The domain symbols Primes, Integers, Rationals, Reals, Complexes, Algebraics, Booleans and PositiveIntegers etc. are used with Element, Reduce, Solve, FindInstance and Assuming to restrict variables (x \[Element] Primes); Reduce over Integers gives all integer solutions of Diophantine problems.
tools.usage:
Element[x, Primes]
Reduce[x^2 + y^2 == 25, {x, y}, Integers]
FindInstance[x^3 + y^3 == z^3 && x > 0 && y > 0 && z > 0, {x, y, z}, Integers]
Solve[p^2 - 2 == q, {p, q}, Primes]
tools.example:
Reduce[2 x + 3 y == 7 && x > 0 && y > 0, {x, y}, Integers]
Solve[x \[Element] Primes && x < 20 && Mod[x, 4] == 1, x]

tools.name: GaussianIntegers
tools.description: Option for FactorInteger, PrimeQ, Factor and related functions: GaussianIntegers -> True works over the Gaussian integers Z[i], so e.g. 5 factors as -I (1+2I)(2+I) and PrimeQ[5] is False. Extension -> Sqrt[2] etc. similarly factors polynomials over algebraic extensions.
tools.usage:
FactorInteger[n, GaussianIntegers -> True]
PrimeQ[n, GaussianIntegers -> True]
Factor[poly, Extension -> Sqrt[2]]
Factor[poly, Modulus -> p]

parameters.name: Extension
parameters.description: Algebraic numbers to adjoin when factoring polynomials.

parameters.name: Modulus
parameters.description: Prime modulus for factoring over finite fields.

tools.example:
FactorInteger[5, GaussianIntegers -> True]
Factor[x^2 - 2, Extension -> Sqrt[2]]
Factor[x^4 + 1, Modulus -> 5]

tools.name: PermutationGroup
tools.description: Represents the group generated by a list of permutations in Cycles form; the object supports GroupOrder, GroupElements, GroupGenerators, GroupOrbits, GroupStabilizer, GroupCentralizer, GroupMultiplicationTable and membership tests (GroupElementQ). Use it for symmetry analysis of graphs, polyhedra and combinatorial structures.
tools.usage:
PermutationGroup[{perm1, perm2, ...}]
GroupOrder[group]
GroupElements[group]
GroupGenerators[group]
GroupElementQ[group, perm]

tools.name: SymmetricGroup
tools.description: Named permutation groups: SymmetricGroup[n], AlternatingGroup[n], CyclicGroup[n], DihedralGroup[n], AbelianGroup[{n1, n2, ...}], plus sporadic groups such as MathieuGroupM11 and the graph automorphism group from GraphAutomorphismGroup. They work with all Group* functions and with Permute to act on lists.
tools.usage:
SymmetricGroup[n]
AlternatingGroup[n]
CyclicGroup[n]
DihedralGroup[n]
AbelianGroup[{n1, n2, ...}]
GraphAutomorphismGroup[g]
tools.example:
GroupOrder[DihedralGroup[6]] (* 12 *)
Permute[{a, b, c}, SymmetricGroup[3]] (* all 6 arrangements *)
GroupElements[CyclicGroup[4]]

tools.name: GroupOrbits
tools.description: GroupOrbits[group, {p1, p2, ...}] gives the orbits of points under the group action; GroupStabilizer[group, {p1, ...}] the subgroup fixing the points pointwise, GroupSetwiseStabilizer the subgroup fixing the set, and GroupCentralizer the centralizer of a permutation. These are the basic orbit-stabilizer computations for counting symmetric configurations (Burnside/Polya).
tools.usage:
GroupOrbits[group]
GroupOrbits[group, {p1, p2, ...}]
GroupStabilizer[group, {p1, ...}]
GroupSetwiseStabilizer[group, {p1, ...}]
GroupCentralizer[group, perm]

tools.name: GroupMultiplicationTable
tools.description: Gives the Cayley (multiplication) table of a permutation group as a matrix of element indices; GroupElementToWord and GroupElementFromWord express elements as words in the generators. Useful for teaching, for verifying isomorphisms and for encoding group elements compactly.
tools.usage:
GroupMultiplicationTable[group]
GroupElementToWord[group, perm]
GroupElementFromWord[group, word]

tools.name: PermutationListQ
tools.description: PermutationListQ tests whether a list is a permutation of Range[n] and PermutationCyclesQ whether an expression is a valid Cycles object; PermutationReplace applies a permutation to integers inside an expression, and PermutationMax/PermutationMin give the largest/smallest moved point. Utility predicates for permutation-based code.
tools.usage:
PermutationListQ[list]
PermutationCyclesQ[expr]
PermutationReplace[expr, perm]
PermutationMax[perm]
PermutationMin[perm]

tools.name: FiniteGroupCount
tools.description: Gives the number of non-isomorphic groups of order n (FiniteAbelianGroupCount for abelian ones), complementing FiniteGroupData which has named groups and their properties. Handy for group-theory exploration and OEIS-style sequences.
tools.usage:
FiniteGroupCount[n]
FiniteAbelianGroupCount[n]

tools.name: PolygonalNumber
tools.description: PolygonalNumber[r, n] gives the n-th r-gonal figurate number (triangular for r = 3, square for 4, pentagonal for 5 ...); related figurate and combinatorial sequences include Fibonacci, LucasL, CatalanNumber, Hyperfactorial, BarnesG, Subfactorial (derangements) and MotzkinNumber-style counts via generating functions. Use them for integer-sequence work.
tools.usage:
PolygonalNumber[n]
PolygonalNumber[r, n]
Subfactorial[n]
Hyperfactorial[n]
tools.example:
PolygonalNumber[5, 10] (* 145 *)
Subfactorial[5] (* 44 derangements *)
Table[PolygonalNumber[n], {n, 10}] (* triangular numbers *)

tools.name: FindLinearRecurrence
tools.description: Finds the minimal linear recurrence with constant coefficients satisfied by a list of numbers (or of vectors/matrices); LinearRecurrence generates terms from a kernel and initial values; FindSequenceFunction guesses a closed form and FindGeneratingFunction a rational generating function. Together they reverse-engineer integer sequences.
tools.usage:
FindLinearRecurrence[list]
LinearRecurrence[{a1, ..., ad}, {y1, ..., yd}, n]
FindSequenceFunction[list, n]
FindGeneratingFunction[list, x]

parameters.name: {a1, ..., ad}
parameters.description: Recurrence kernel y[n] = a1 y[n-1] + ... + ad y[n-d].

tools.example:
FindLinearRecurrence[{1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13}] (* {1, 1} *)
LinearRecurrence[{1, 1}, {1, 1}, 10]
FindSequenceFunction[{1, 4, 9, 16, 25}, n] (* n^2 *)
FindGeneratingFunction[{1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8}, x]
